# Hands-on with Agent Auth (AAuth)

Run every party of AAuth on one machine, give two agents cryptographic identities, and watch a downstream resource learn the whole chain of who asked whom, with every hop and every token in Jaeger. Deep dives on delegation, the six access modes, and what the act claim carries.

**[▶ Take this lab on the Zenable Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=aauth-agent-authorization&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=aauth-agent-authorization_readme)** — fully hosted sandbox environment, progress tracking, and a full-featured lab workspace.

**Duration** 2 hours · **Difficulty** Intermediate

**Topics** `Agent Identity` · `Security`

**Prerequisites**

- Docker and git
- uv, jq and curl
- Comfort with HTTP, JSON, and the shell
- A working knowledge of OAuth 2.0 (you should know what a bearer token is)

---

_This README is only the hands-on lab. The concept walk-through (Welcome, Setup, and Terminology · Deep Dive: Sending Someone Else to Do a Job · Deep Dive: Six Ways to Prove Who Is Calling · Deep Dive: What the Signature Covers · Deep Dive: What AAuth Does Not Solve · Epilogue: The Public Internet · Conclusion) lives on the [Learning Hub](https://www.zenable.app/learn?lab=aauth-agent-authorization&utm_source=github&utm_medium=labs_repo&utm_campaign=aauth-agent-authorization_readme)._

## Hands-on: Enrol an Agent

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Time to become an agent. Enrolling generates two Ed25519 keys, a stable one that is your identity across restarts and a signing one for this session, and registers the stable key with the Agent Server. A person then approves the registration, and the Agent Server issues an `agent_token` bound to your signing key.

```bash
uv run python agent.py register
```

```console
POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/register -> 202
  location: /register/pending/KrjLrfBoGTEUMvibzckiMA
enrolment pending: approve it at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ui/portal.html then run register again
```

A `202`, and nothing issued yet. Registering is a request to a person, and nobody has said yes. Open the portal at http://localhost:8765/ui/portal.html, sign in with `lab`, and look under **Pending registrations**. You'll find two: `lab-agent`, which is you, and `relay`, which enrolled itself when its container started. The relay is a resource that will act as an agent later, so it needs an identity of its own.

Approve both in the portal, or do the same thing from the shell. The portal's own API takes the same token:

```bash
for id in $(curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/registrations \
  | jq -r '.[] | select(.status == "pending") | .id'); do
  curl -s -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' "http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/registrations/${id}/approve" | jq -c .
done
```

```console
$ for id in $(curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/registrations \
>   | jq -r '.[] | select(.status == "pending") | .id'); do
>   curl -s -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' "http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/registrations/${id}/approve" | jq -c .
> done
{"agent_id":"aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example","agent_name":"relay"}
{"agent_id":"aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example","agent_name":"lab-agent"}
```

Each approval mints an agent identifier, `aauth:<id>@<domain>`. Now finish your enrolment; the agent polls the pending registration it remembers, and this time the answer is a token:

```bash
uv run python agent.py register  # the same command; the approval is in now
```

```console
GET http://127.0.0.1:8765/register/pending/KrjLrfBoGTEUMvibzckiMA -> 200
enrolled as aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
```

Read what the Agent Server said about you:

```bash
uv run python agent.py whoami
```

```console
{
  "iss": "http://127.0.0.1:8765",
  "sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example",
  "dwk": "aauth-agent.json",
  "jti": "893f8486-8b01-42b7-9904-bd5516f06367",
  "cnf": {
    "jwk": {
      "kty": "OKP",
      "crv": "Ed25519",
      "x": "DlHSUADR7EXfbmi5f4IhzYUecwC5v7ecu80FeUK4ILY"
    }
  },
  "iat": 1791210567,
  "exp": 1791296967,
  "ps": "http://127.0.0.1:8765"
}
```

That's your `agent_token`, decoded. `sub` is who you are, `cnf.jwk` is the public half of the key you sign with, and `ps` names the Person Server that speaks for the person you work for. A resource that trusts this Agent Server can verify your signature with nothing more than `iss` and the key the token vouches for. Your identifier shows up in the portal under **Active agents** too.

Success! Your private keys are in `~/.aauth-lab/`, outside the lab directory, so nothing private rides along if the directory gets copied.

> [!TIP]
> Compare this with an API key. A key has to be *given* to the resource, which means the resource can now impersonate you to anyone else who accepts that key. Your public key can be handed to the world, and only you can still sign.

## Hands-on: The Identity-Based Call

_~12 min · Hands-on_

This is the simplest AAuth exchange there is: one request, one response, no person, and no consent. Knock on the relay first without an identity, so you can see what it says to a stranger:

```bash
curl --silent --show-error --include http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
```

```console
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
www-authenticate: AAuth
content-type: application/json
aauth-requirement: requirement=auth-token
signature-error: error=invalid_signature
accept-signature: sig2=("@method" "@authority" "@path");sigkey=uri
content-length: 29
date: Mon, 05 Oct 2026 14:29:40 GMT

{"error":"missing_signature"}
```

No login page, no API key form, no "register your application". Look at `accept-signature`: the refusal names the components it wants covered, so a caller who has never seen this service before still knows what to sign.

Now call as yourself:

```bash
uv run python agent.py call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
```

```console
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 200
{
  "relay_saw": {
    "x-aauth-level": "identified",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "http://127.0.0.1:8765",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-jkt": "d7gaqeSGDcoeGI0ZKd3ZBrCqMZpaQjFq8yv0ynp7AwA"
  },
  "downstream_status": 200,
  "downstream_saw": {
    "x-aauth-level": "identified",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "http://127.0.0.1:8765",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-jkt": "npmDw-d3UEan0TmYGztD1-K3rOCc80jJgyYstpQIt1k"
  },
  "downstream_act": null
}
```

The relay answers with two views. `relay_saw` is what the gateway stamped on your request after `aauth-service` verified it: level `identified`, and `x-aauth-delegate` is your agent identifier. The relay then called `echo` as itself, and `downstream_saw` is what echo got: level `identified` again, but the delegate is the *relay's* identifier. Echo has no idea you exist. `downstream_act` is empty because nothing in identity-based mode carries a chain.

Hold onto that gap. It's the whole reason the `act` claim exists, and the next hands-on section closes it.

Now the trace. Every service in the stack exports to Jaeger, and `trace.sh` prints the newest trace your agent started, one line per hop with any AAuth claims that hop put on its span:

```bash
./trace.sh
```

```console
agent         agent call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
                aauth.agent.iss = http://127.0.0.1:8765
                aauth.agent.sub = aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
agent         GET                                     200
agentgateway  GET /*                                  200
relay         GET /relay                              200
                aauth.inbound.iss = http://127.0.0.1:8765
                aauth.inbound.sub = aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
                x-aauth-agent-server = http://127.0.0.1:8765
                x-aauth-delegate = aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
                x-aauth-jkt = d7gaqeSGDcoeGI0ZKd3ZBrCqMZpaQjFq8yv0ynp7AwA
                x-aauth-level = identified
relay         GET                                     200
agentgateway  GET /*                                  200
```

One trace, four services. Your agent's root span carries the claims of the token it signed with. The gateway's span is the request as the resource saw it. The relay's span carries the headers it was handed, and then its own outbound hop and the gateway again for echo. The `traceparent` header your agent sent is what stitched them together: each service picked it up, added its spans, and passed it on.

<details>
<summary>What's a span?</summary>

A span is a single timed piece of work. It has a name, a start and end time, a set of key-value attributes, and usually a parent. A trace is a tree of spans that share one trace id. Here the root span is your command, and every HTTP request below it, in whichever service, is a child of that root.

</details>

Open Chromium from the sandbox desktop and go to **http://localhost:16686**. Pick `agent` in the Service dropdown and hit Find Traces. Click the newest one and you'll see the same tree as a timeline, with each service in its own colour. Click a span to see the attributes `trace.sh` printed. Keep that tab open; from here on, every step ends there.

## Hands-on: The act Claim

_~16 min · Hands-on_

Now switch both resources to the three-party flow. The second config tells `aauth-service` that an agent token is no longer enough: a request has to carry an `auth_token` from the Person Server. The service reads its config once at start, so restart it:

```bash
cp 02-auth-token.yaml aauth-config.yaml
docker compose restart aauth-service
docker compose up -d --wait aauth-service
```

```console
$ cp 02-auth-token.yaml aauth-config.yaml
$ docker compose restart aauth-service
$ docker compose up -d --wait aauth-service
```

Call the relay again:

```bash
uv run python agent.py call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
```

```console
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 401
  aauth-requirement: requirement=auth-token, resource-token="eyJ0eXAiOiJhYS1yZXNvdXJjZStqd3QiLCJhbGciOiJFZERTQSIsImtp...
  www-authenticate: AAuth
POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/token -> 200
auth token issued by http://127.0.0.1:8765 for http://127.0.0.1:3000: agent=aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example act={"sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example"}
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 200
{
  "relay_saw": {
    "x-aauth-scope": "relay:read",
    "x-aauth-jkt": "d7gaqeSGDcoeGI0ZKd3ZBrCqMZpaQjFq8yv0ynp7AwA",
    "x-aauth-level": "authorized",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "user"
  },
  "downstream_status": 200,
  "downstream_saw": {
    "x-aauth-jkt": "npmDw-d3UEan0TmYGztD1-K3rOCc80jJgyYstpQIt1k",
    "x-aauth-level": "authorized",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "user",
    "x-aauth-scope": "echo:read"
  },
  "downstream_act": {
    "sub": "aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example",
    "act": {
      "sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example"
    }
  }
}
delegation chain, outermost first:
  aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example
    aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
```

Three things happened on your side, and the same three again on the relay's side. Read yours first:

1. **The 401.** Your agent-token call came back refused, carrying a `resource_token`. The relay just told you, in a signed object, exactly what decision it needs and who should make it: its `aud` is the Person Server.
2. **The exchange.** Your agent posted that token to the Person Server. The response is an `auth_token` for `http://127.0.0.1:3000`, with `agent` set to you and `act` set to `{"sub": you}`. For a direct call, the actor is the agent that asked.
3. **The retry.** The same request, now signed with the `auth_token`, and the level is `authorized`. `x-aauth-delegate` is `user`, the person this Person Server speaks for, and `x-aauth-scope` is what the token grants.

Then the relay did the same dance with echo, and this is the part to look at. When echo refused the relay, the relay took echo's `resource_token` to the Person Server together with the `auth_token` *it had been called with*, as an upstream token. The Person Server verified both, and the auth token it issued for echo carries `act` nested one level deep: the relay, and inside it, you. `downstream_act` is that claim, and the chain printed under it is what echo can now read: a request from the relay, on your behalf, for the person.

Now the trace:

```bash
./trace.sh
```

```console
agent         agent call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
                aauth.agent.iss = http://127.0.0.1:8765
                aauth.agent.sub = aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
                aauth.auth.act = {"sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example"}
                aauth.auth.agent = aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
                aauth.auth.aud = http://127.0.0.1:3000
                aauth.auth.iss = http://127.0.0.1:8765
                aauth.auth.scope = relay:read
                aauth.auth.sub = user
agent         GET                                     401
agentgateway  GET /*                                  401
agent         GET                                     200
person-server GET /.well-known/aauth-person.json      200
agent         POST                                    200
person-server POST /token                             200
agent         GET                                     200
agentgateway  GET /*                                  200
relay         GET /relay                              200
                aauth.downstream.act = {"sub": "aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example", "act": {"sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example"}}
                aauth.downstream.agent = aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example
                aauth.downstream.aud = http://127.0.0.1:3001
                aauth.downstream.iss = http://127.0.0.1:8765
                aauth.downstream.scope = echo:read
                aauth.downstream.sub = user
                aauth.inbound.act = {"sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example"}
                aauth.inbound.agent = aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
                aauth.inbound.aud = http://127.0.0.1:3000
                aauth.inbound.iss = http://127.0.0.1:8765
                aauth.inbound.scope = relay:read
                aauth.inbound.sub = user
                x-aauth-agent-server = aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
                x-aauth-delegate = user
                x-aauth-jkt = d7gaqeSGDcoeGI0ZKd3ZBrCqMZpaQjFq8yv0ynp7AwA
                x-aauth-level = authorized
                x-aauth-scope = relay:read
relay         GET                                     401
agentgateway  GET /*                                  401
relay         GET                                     200
person-server GET /.well-known/aauth-person.json      200
relay         POST                                    200
person-server POST /token                             200
relay         GET                                     200
agentgateway  GET /*                                  200
```

This is the picture the lab is about. Eighteen hops across four services, in one trace, and the tokens on the spans that held them. Follow `act` down the page: on your root span it names you. On the relay's span, `aauth.inbound.act` is that same token as the relay received it, and `aauth.downstream.act` is the token the relay obtained, with your `act` nested inside its own. Open the same trace in the Jaeger tab and click the relay's `GET /relay` span: those attributes are there, and the Person Server's `POST /token` spans sit on the timeline exactly where each exchange happened.

**Question**: the relay held your `auth_token` and could have signed its request to echo with it directly, skipping the Person Server. Why does the protocol make it exchange instead?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Because your `auth_token` is bound to *your* key. Its `cnf.jwk` is the public half of the key you sign with, and `aud` is the relay. Echo would refuse it twice over: the audience is wrong, and the relay can't produce a signature that matches the confirmation key.

The exchange is what lets the relay act as itself while still carrying the fact that it acts for you. It signs with its own key, the token names it in `agent` and `act.sub`, and your identity rides inside `act.act`. Nobody along the way needed your private key, and echo can still see the whole chain.

</details>

> [!WARNING]
> A nested `act` records who asked. It says nothing about whether what they asked for was in scope. Containment across hops, showing that each hop stayed inside the original grant, is still an open design question in the draft.

## Hands-on: Consent

_~12 min · Hands-on_

So far the Person Server has said yes on its own. The third config adds `require:user` to the relay's resource token, which tells the Person Server to ask its person before issuing. Echo keeps its autonomous config, so the relay's chained exchange needs no second approval.

Switch, and forget the auth tokens your agent is holding, because a token issued under the old config is still a valid token until it expires:

```bash
cp 03-consent.yaml aauth-config.yaml
docker compose restart aauth-service
docker compose up -d --wait aauth-service
uv run python agent.py forget
uv run python agent.py call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
```

```console
$ cp 03-consent.yaml aauth-config.yaml
$ docker compose restart aauth-service
$ docker compose up -d --wait aauth-service
$ uv run python agent.py forget
auth tokens forgotten
$ uv run python agent.py call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 401
  aauth-requirement: requirement=auth-token, resource-token="eyJ0eXAiOiJhYS1yZXNvdXJjZStqd3QiLCJhbGciOiJFZERTQSIsImtp...
  www-authenticate: AAuth
POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/token -> 202
  aauth-requirement: requirement=interaction; url="http://127.0.0.1:8765/ui/consent.html"; code="pP1UYL75onbl8uYe2ZwY...
  location: http://127.0.0.1:8765/pending/ju_KTUvATxS2pfy
a person has to approve this: open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ui/consent.html?code=pP1UYL75onbl8uYe2ZwY4A then run call again
```

The exchange came back `202` instead of `200`. The Person Server has a pending decision, a `location` to poll, and an `AAuth-Requirement` that says what has to happen first: a person opens that URL. This is the only human step in the entire protocol.

Open the consent link from the output in Chromium. The page names the agent asking, the resource it wants, and the scope. Approve it. The same decision is one API call, which is what the next block does; run it if you'd rather stay in the shell:

```bash
for id in $(curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' http://127.0.0.1:8765/admin/pending \
  | jq -r '.[] | select(.kind == "token" and .status != "resolved") | .pending_id'); do
  curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"approved": true}' \
    "http://127.0.0.1:8765/consent/${id}/decision"; echo " approved ${id}"
done
```

```console
$ for id in $(curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' http://127.0.0.1:8765/admin/pending \
>   | jq -r '.[] | select(.kind == "token" and .status != "resolved") | .pending_id'); do
>   curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"approved": true}' \
>     "http://127.0.0.1:8765/consent/${id}/decision"; echo " approved ${id}"
> done
{} approved ju_KTUvATxS2pfy
```

Then call again. The agent remembers the pending exchange and polls it instead of starting over:

```bash
uv run python agent.py call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
```

```console
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 401
  aauth-requirement: requirement=auth-token, resource-token="eyJ0eXAiOiJhYS1yZXNvdXJjZStqd3QiLCJhbGciOiJFZERTQSIsImtp...
  www-authenticate: AAuth
GET http://127.0.0.1:8765/pending/ju_KTUvATxS2pfy -> 200
auth token issued by http://127.0.0.1:8765 for http://127.0.0.1:3000: agent=aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example act={"sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example"}
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 200
{
  "relay_saw": {
    "x-aauth-jkt": "d7gaqeSGDcoeGI0ZKd3ZBrCqMZpaQjFq8yv0ynp7AwA",
    "x-aauth-level": "authorized",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "user",
    "x-aauth-scope": "relay:read require:user"
  },
  "downstream_status": 200,
  "downstream_saw": {
    "x-aauth-level": "authorized",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "user",
    "x-aauth-scope": "echo:read",
    "x-aauth-jkt": "npmDw-d3UEan0TmYGztD1-K3rOCc80jJgyYstpQIt1k"
  },
  "downstream_act": {
    "sub": "aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example",
    "act": {
      "sub": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example"
    }
  }
}
delegation chain, outermost first:
  aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example
    aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example
```

The `200` on the poll is the moment authorization was created; everything before it was negotiation. The scope now carries `require:user`, the relay's exchange went through without a second question, and the chain echo sees is the same two agents as before. In Jaeger this trace has a gap in the middle, between the `POST /token` that answered `202` and the poll that answered `200`, and the gap is exactly how long the person took.

**Question**: the resource just received a person's identity, `user`, and a scope. It has never met that person, and it never asked them for anything. Why is it willing to believe the token?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Because the agent didn't assert any of it. The Person Server did, and it signed the token that carries it.

The resource pins the Person Server it trusts in its config, fetches that server's JWKS, and verifies the signature over those claims. So the question the resource actually answered is "do I trust this Person Server", which is a decision it makes once, about one issuer, rather than per request about an agent it has never seen.

Compare that to an API key with a `user_id` field in the request body. Any agent can claim to be acting for anyone. Forging a Person Server's signature is a different problem entirely.

</details>

## Hands-on: Ways to Be Refused

_~12 min · Hands-on_

Auth code that has only ever been tested with a good token is untested code. Each of these should fail, and the interesting part of each one is the *reason* it fails, or the one case where it doesn't.

**1. The replayed signature.** `sign` prints the headers of one signed request, so you can send it by hand with `curl`, outside the agent. Send it twice:

```bash
uv run python agent.py sign http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo > /tmp/signed-request
curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}\n' -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo
curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}\n' -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo
```

```console
$ uv run python agent.py sign http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo > /tmp/signed-request
$ curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}\n' -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo
401
$ curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}\n' -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo
401
```

Both refused, and before you read that as replay protection, look at why: echo is still in three-party mode, and this request carries your agent token, which isn't enough any more. The replay question is about the signature, so ask it where a signature is enough. Put the resources back in identity mode for a moment:

```bash
cp 01-identity.yaml aauth-config.yaml
docker compose restart aauth-service
docker compose up -d --wait aauth-service
uv run python agent.py sign http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo > /tmp/signed-request
for attempt in first second; do
  curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out "${attempt}: %{http_code}\n" -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo
done
```

```console
$ cp 01-identity.yaml aauth-config.yaml
$ docker compose restart aauth-service
$ docker compose up -d --wait aauth-service
$ uv run python agent.py sign http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo > /tmp/signed-request
$ for attempt in first second; do
>   curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out "${attempt}: %{http_code}\n" -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo
> done
first: 200
second: 200
```

Accepted twice. This resource checks the `created` timestamp against a sixty-second window and keeps no record of what it has seen, so a byte-for-byte replay inside the window is a valid request. That is the checkpoint answer from the deep dive playing out for real. Whether a verifier keeps a seen-list is its own decision, and it's one to ask about before you put a signature-verifying proxy in front of anything that changes state.

**2. The signature aimed at the wrong target.** Take the same flags and send them to a different path on the same host:

```bash
curl --silent --include -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/not-echo | grep -i 'HTTP/\|error'
```

```console
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
signature-error: error=invalid_signature
{"error":"invalid_signature"}
```

Refused. `@path` is inside the signature base, so the proof doesn't transfer even though the clock would have allowed it.

**3. The stale signature.** Wait out the window, then send the original once more:

```bash
sleep 61
curl --silent --include -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo | grep -i 'HTTP/\|error\|date'
```

```console
$ sleep 61
$ curl --silent --include -H @/tmp/signed-request http://127.0.0.1:3001/echo | grep -i 'HTTP/\|error\|date'
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
signature-error: error=invalid_signature
date: Mon, 05 Oct 2026 14:32:20 GMT
{"error":"invalid_signature"}
```

Refused, for the reason the deep dive promised: `created` is now outside the window.

**4. The revoked agent.** Revoke the relay's binding at the Person Server, in the portal under **Active agents**, or from the shell, then call the relay again:

```bash
for id in $(curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/bindings \
  | jq -r '.[] | select(.agent_name == "relay") | .agent_id'); do
  curl -s -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' "http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/bindings/${id}/revoke"; echo " revoked ${id}"
done
uv run python agent.py call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
```

```console
$ for id in $(curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/bindings \
>   | jq -r '.[] | select(.agent_name == "relay") | .agent_id'); do
>   curl -s -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab' "http://127.0.0.1:8765/person/bindings/${id}/revoke"; echo " revoked ${id}"
> done
 revoked aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example
$ uv run python agent.py call http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 401
  aauth-requirement: requirement=auth-token
  signature-error: error=invalid_jwt
  www-authenticate: AAuth
GET http://127.0.0.1:3000/relay -> 200
{
  "relay_saw": {
    "x-aauth-level": "identified",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "http://127.0.0.1:8765",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "aauth:1b02fcec-e207-4422-9d5c-5777f66d2bab@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-jkt": "d7gaqeSGDcoeGI0ZKd3ZBrCqMZpaQjFq8yv0ynp7AwA"
  },
  "downstream_status": 200,
  "downstream_saw": {
    "x-aauth-level": "identified",
    "x-aauth-agent-server": "http://127.0.0.1:8765",
    "x-aauth-delegate": "aauth:857f2e4e-7cd6-4afc-8743-e9c4975a9b15@agent-server.example",
    "x-aauth-jkt": "npmDw-d3UEan0TmYGztD1-K3rOCc80jJgyYstpQIt1k"
  },
  "downstream_act": null
}
```

Read the two `GET` lines first. The agent still held the auth token from the consent section, the resources are back in identity mode where an auth token is the wrong kind of credential, so the first call was refused and the agent fell back to its agent token. The relay did the same with echo. Then `200`, and the relay still reached echo. The resource verified the relay's agent token against the Agent Server's JWKS, and that token is valid for twenty-four hours from when it was issued. Revoking the binding stops the Person Server from issuing anything new to that agent; it does nothing to the tokens already in the relay's memory. This is the second of the five problems from the delegation deep dive, in a form you can see: withdrawing permission and stopping work are different events, and the distance between them here is a token lifetime.

Success! Four tests, and a less tidy set of answers than a slide would give you: two refusals, one replay that worked, and one revocation that didn't stop anything. Each one is a check you'd have to write, or configure, yourself if you were building the resource side.

## What to Take Back to Work

_~4 min · Discussion_

Concretely, in order of effort:

1. **Inventory your machine-to-machine keys.** Every long-lived API key an agent holds is a candidate for identity-based mode. You don't need consent, a Person Server, or an Access Server to replace one.
2. **Find the calls where "who asked for this" is currently a field in the request body.** An `act` chain would make those trustworthy instead of merely stated.
3. **Find every place one of your services calls another on a caller's behalf.** Each is a relay, and each one today drops the chain. Decide which of them should carry it.
4. **Put the tokens in your traces.** Today's trace showed every hop and every claim because each service put them on its spans. That's an afternoon of work per service, and it's the difference between a log line and the picture you had today.
5. **Write down which of the five open problems you're carrying.** For each one, name the control outside AAuth that covers it today, even if that control is a human reading a log on Mondays.

## Cleanup

_~3 min · Hands-on_

Stop the stack, drop the Person Server's database with it, and forget your agent's keys:

```bash
docker compose down -v
uv run python agent.py reset
```

```console
$ docker compose down -v
$ uv run python agent.py reset
forgotten
```
